summary: Technical deep-dive on private/VPC deployment security for Midland Systems. Focus areas: ingress/egress controls, outbound proxy and firewall strategy, RBAC/SSO integration, KMS key management and audit log retention for SOC 2 readiness. Agreed on sending artifacts and running a short egress benchmark; next meeting to focus on KMS rotation and operator roles.
topics: firewalling patterns and service mesh tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to walk through the private deploy security picture and make sure we've captured your constraints. I see James, Marta, Liam, thanks for the time.

[00:18] James (Midland CTO): yeah thanks Alex, quick agenda ask — we want to validate that the control plane can be isolated and that egress is fully controlled, also KMS handoff is a hard requirement for us.

[00:32] Priya (Redwood SE): perfect. we'll start with the high level — Redwood Private has a customer-controlled VPC and optional on-prem runtime, the control plane can be run as a private VPC endpoint or customer-managed instance, and all egress can be routed through either our managed egress proxy or your own outbound gateway. note: sometimes transcribers render KV cache as K V cache, sorry about that.

[01:00] Marta (Head of Security): couple of hard constraints from compliance — SOC2 audit wants immutable audit logs kept for 1 year in our EU bucket, SSO via SAML for RBAC with SCIM sync, and HSM-backed KMS with key rotation under our tenancy.

[01:20] Daniel (Redwood Prod Sec): yep we support customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-key) and integration with common HSM/KMS providers. rotation can be automated but we'd like to align the rotation window with your key custody policy — we also expose encrypted audit logs to your s3/GCS bucket in pre-defined formats.

[01:44] Liam (Platform Eng): when you say audit logs, is that request/response payloads or just control plane telemetry? we have PII considerations so we cannot ship full request payloads outside the VPC.

[02:02] Priya (Redwood SE): good call — we support two modes: 1) control plane telemetry and structured request metadata (prompt hashes, token counts, latencies) sent to your retention bucket, or 2) full payload capture if you opt into that and keep it on-prem. commonly customers choose metadata-only for SOC2 and keep raw payloads internal.

[02:26] James: ok that aligns. next up is egress — we need to ensure that model artifacts, downloads, and any cloud calls only go to our allowlist. can Redwood run in a mode where DNS resolves are blocked except to configured endpoints?

[02:42] Alex: yes — Private runtime supports a deny-by-default egress policy. you provide the CIDR/host list; we recommend an egress proxy in front of external calls, with TLS inspection optional on your side. Redwood can also publish signed manifests for model artifacts so the runtime only pulls pinned checksums from allowed artifact mirrors.

[03:03] Marta: pinned checksums are crucial. how do updates / patching work? we need a way to review changes for SOC2 evidence.

[03:12] Daniel: we have release manifests and a signed changelog plus a security bulletin. for Private we can expose a lock-step rollout where you approve new runtime images before they pull — that's an opt-in workflow. we'll capture approval events in the audit logs.

[03:28] Speaker 4 (SRE): there's also network-level segmentation concerns — do you recommend a service mesh or a single-proxy pattern for internal egress to the model-serving pool?

[03:36] Priya: tradeoffs — service meshes give mTLS and per-service policies but add complexity and observability overhead; single egress proxy is simpler and often meets SOC2 if you pair it with RBAC and strict SGs (security groups). For high-scale LLM workloads we typically recommend a lightweight proxy + ACLs to avoid per-request sidecars latency.

[04:00] Liam: latency is a big deal for us — can you quantify added tail latency for an egress proxy in-line with your batching engine?

[04:08] Priya: rough numbers — we see 5–12 ms added per-request for an optimized egress proxy on modern hardware, but it depends on TLS renegotiation and packet path. we'll run a benchmark with your sample traffic and give CSVs.

[04:26] James: nice. on RBAC — we need role separation between developer, ops, and compliance auditor. our auditors should be read-only and not able to trigger model rollouts. can Redwood map SAML groups to granular roles?

[04:40] Alex: yes — SAML + SCIM provisioning to map groups into roles. we support fine-grained roles (read-only auditor, deployer, operator). SCIM sync can be one-way and limited. note: sometimes the SAML attributes are munged in export; we'll provide a sample SAML metadata file to validate mapping.

[04:59] Marta: what about emergency access? our DR plan requires break-glass keys for the control plane but we need full auditability when they're used.

[05:10] Daniel: break-glass is supported with time-limited tokens and full event logging. we can require multi-party approval via your internal tool before unlocking and record the approvers in audit logs.

[05:26] Ellen (Legal): quick legal note — we need to review the data processing addendum and ensure KMS terms allow customer-controlled key destruction.

[05:34] Alex: we'll attach our DPA and the recommended edits in the follow-up.

[05:40] Priya: jumping back to egress controls — two patterns customers use: 1) customer-hosted outbound gateway (recommended when you want full control) or 2) Redwood-managed egress with allowlist and upstream peering. both can be combined with mutual TLS.

[06:00] James: for us customer-hosted is preferred. what are the ops expectations? like, who handles cert rotation and monitoring?

[06:09] Priya: if it's customer-hosted, Midland controls certs, rotation, and monitoring; Redwood will handshake with that gateway via mTLS using a cert we provision into the runtime, or you can rotate on your side and provide the CA bundle. we'll provide a small operator playbook.

[06:27] Liam: and what about model downloads? we'd prefer storing model artifacts in our internal blobstore and forbidding outbound DNS to public registries.

[06:36] Daniel: supported — you can point Redwood to your artifact mirror. we support verifying SHA256 checksums and GPG signatures. the runtime will refuse to start a model if the checksum doesn't match.

[06:48] James: can you capture an example of the audit log format? we need something our SIEM can consume.

[06:55] Alex: yes, we'll send sample logs (JSON lines) — fields include event_time, actor, action, resource, outcome, request_hash, token_count, latency_ms. we'll make sure the schema matches common SIEM parsers.

[07:10] Marta: retention and encryption at rest for logs? 

[07:14] Daniel: logs can be pushed encrypted to your S3 bucket with SSE-KMS (your key), or we can store them in your on-prem ELK via secure forwarder. retention is configurable; SOC2 recommended one year but we can do custom windows.

[07:28] Alex: quick note on data residency — if you need EU-only processing, we can pin the runtime to EU regions and ensure artifacts and logs never egress to US locations. just need to set the region policy in the control plane config.

[07:42] James: perfect. one more operational: what does the rollback/canary process look like if a model regression hits production?

[07:50] Priya: canary rollouts are supported — you can route X% of traffic to the new model, monitor quality signals and error rates, and auto-fallback if thresholds breach. all of those events are logged for audit. you can also pin a specific model version in the config to avoid auto-updates.

[08:06] Speaker 4: are there any known SOC2 gaps for the default private deploy config?

[08:11] Daniel: default is mostly SOC2-friendly but customers need to ensure network controls on their side (NAC, egress firewall rules), and that KMS keys are customer-controlled. we'll include a SOC2 readiness checklist showing any control that requires customer action.

[08:26] Marta: great, can we see the checklist today?

[08:29] Alex: i'll send it after the call along with the SOC2 Type II PDF and a sample audit log.

[08:35] James: cool. let's walk through a quick hypothetical: SRE triggers a model deploy, traffic spikes, egress gateway gets saturated — what's the mitigation?

[08:46] Priya: mitigation options: rate-limit external artifact download, scale egress gateway horizontally, or fail closed-back to a local cache. we also support priority queues for control-plane ops so critical calls don't get starved.

[08:59] Liam: and how do we test the break-glass flow without impacting production?

[09:05] Daniel: we suggest a staging account with the same policy and a scheduled simulated break-glass exercise recorded for auditors. we can help run the simulation.

[09:16] James: ok that's helpful. i'm going to hand back to Marta for any final questions.

[09:21] Marta: couple quick ones — rotation cadence for KMS, and do you support asymmetric key wrapping?

[09:28] Daniel: rotation cadence is configurable; we can support daily to annual rotations. we support envelope encryption with asymmetric key wrapping where your HSM holds the master key and Redwood uses wrapped data keys — common pattern for enterprise.

[09:42] Marta: lovely. last ask: can Redwood provide an immutable proof that a particular model version saw only EU-region inference? some of our customers will audit that.

[09:51] Priya: yes we produce region-bound execution logs that include node_id, AZ, and region tag; signed manifests per-request can be enabled. that should satisfy auditors.

[10:05] Alex: ok wrapping up — action items as we listed, we'll share the docs and run the benchmark. any other blockers?

[10:13] James: none from me. thanks all.

[10:16] Ellen (Legal): i will follow up with comments to the DPA.

[10:20] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll follow up by EOD with the checklist, SOC2 artefacts, and timeline for the benchmark.

[10:28] (call ends)

Notes: transcript has occasional mislabels and imperfect punctuation; attachments referenced: private-deploy-checklist.pdf (link will be shared), soc2-typeii-2025.pdf (link), egress-benchmark-template.csv (link).
